title: On two differing geometric descriptions of the passage from microscopy to macroscopy in Markov diffusion theory
abstract: In various disparate settings one studies how random processes give way to parabolic partial differential equations and in turn to functional inequalities involving gradients and variational calculus. Particles subject to gradient forces, the fields which move them, the empirical measures which they form, the smooth laws which those measures approximate, and differentiable functionals of these laws constitute a hierarchy of descriptions of diffusion. Intervening on this hierarchy is a choice of how a conintuity operator converts particle velocity to the evolution of measures. Here a central object is constructed mediating two different such descriptions. The space of smooth positive probability densities on a closed Riemannian manifold is treated as a Fréchet manifold whose full continuous cotangent space consists of nonconstant distributions and whose regular cotangent space consists of sufficiently regular nonconstant functions. Beginning from the operator on this space arising as the infinitesimal lift of diffeomorphisms of the base manifold, two different Hilbert completions of this space of densities account for a wide class of objects relevant, leading to a partial universalisation of the microscopic--mesoscopic--macroscopic hierarchy in Markov analysis.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework comparing two distinct geometric descriptions—Otto and Stein—for how particle random walks transition into macroscopic diffusion equations on a manifold. It achieves this by treating the space of probability densities as an infinite-dimensional manifold, showing that agreement between these physical descriptions requires satisfying specific differential geometric identities.
main_problem: The central problem is rigorously characterizing the mathematical passage from microscopic descriptions of particle random processes to macroscopic continuum descriptions, such as parabolic partial differential equations, within Markov diffusion theory.
main_result: The paper establishes that two distinct geometric frameworks—the Otto geometry and the Stein geometry—arise depending on the choice of norm for admissible velocities. Agreement between these two descriptions is governed by a specific condition involving the operator M_rho grad f = grad f.
method: The authors utilize advanced differential geometry, treating the space of smooth probability densities as a Fréchet manifold. They compare geometric structures (tangent/cotangent spaces) derived from different Hilbert completions and employ tools from optimal transport theory.
model_or_system: The model concerns diffusion processes on a closed Riemannian manifold, where particles move under gradient forces and their empirical measures approximate smooth probability densities ($ho$). The analysis focuses on the continuity operator linking particle velocity to measure evolution.
key_observables: Probability density $ho$, particle velocity fields $v$, relative entropy, dissipation costs, and geometric structures like the Otto and Stein tangent spaces.
important_parameters: The geometry of the underlying Riemannian manifold, the regularity/smoothness of the density ($\inf ho > 0$), and the choice of norm used for completion (e.g., weighted $L^2(ho)$ vs. kernel norm).
main_assumptions: The analysis often requires assuming sufficient smoothness or boundedness away from zero for the probability density to ensure uniform ellipticity and well-defined geometric structures.
paper_structure: The paper builds a hierarchy connecting particle dynamics (microscopic) through measure evolution (mesoscopic) to functional inequalities (macroscopic). It systematically compares the mathematical implications of different choices in this continuity operator, culminating in explicit equivalence conditions.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, understanding how geometric structures derived from physical processes (like diffusion) relate to underlying microscopic dynamics is fundamental. The comparison between established variational/geometric frameworks (Otto vs. Stein) provides a powerful mathematical tool for analyzing non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models.
